summary:
AERIS is a data-driven agricultural decision-support platform developed to evaluate crop feasibility across the Nashik district of Maharashtra.

We developed a hybrid feasibility engine that integrates geospatial, soil and environmental datasets to assess agricultural suitability. Using Python-based data processing, we transform complex raster datasets into structured, analysable formats, clean inconsistencies, handle missing values and derive meaningful statistical indicators. These parameters are processed through a weighted evaluation model and a Genetic Algorithm to explore and rank feasible agricultural candidates.

AERIS addresses the challenge of fragmented agricultural data and uncertain crop-selection decisions by bringing multiple environmental factors into a unified analytical framework. Rather than relying on isolated parameters or general recommendations, it provides geographically relevant, data-backed assessments.

Our goal is to make agricultural planning more informed, scientifically grounded and accessible, helping bridge the gap between raw environmental data and practical decision-making. It connects traditional knowledge with modern data.
details:
AERIS – Agricultural Environmental Recommendation and Intelligence System

AERIS is a data-driven agricultural decision-support system designed to help farmers make more informed decisions about crop selection and crop rotation. Developed with a focus on Nashik district, Maharashtra, the project brings together environmental data, geospatial analysis and an optimisation algorithm to identify crop combinations that are better suited to the available environmental conditions.

The system begins by collecting and processing geographical and environmental datasets, including soil properties such as pH, clay, sand, organic carbon, nitrogen and cation exchange capacity, along with terrain information such as elevation, slope and aspect. These datasets are processed using Python libraries and converted into structured, comparable values. Using the official district boundary, Nashik is divided into 15 spatial management cells. Each cell receives an environmental profile based on the available raster data, allowing the system to evaluate different parts of the district independently rather than treating the entire region as having identical soil conditions.

AERIS then evaluates the suitability of different crops using factors such as soil pH, soil texture and slope. It also incorporates a rainfall outlook derived from historical rainfall patterns at a Nashik climate reference point. The resulting crop suitability scores are used by a Genetic Algorithm to explore possible three-season crop rotations across Kharif, Rabi and Summer. The algorithm evaluates combinations based on their average crop suitability and rotation compatibility, while applying penalties to discourage unsuitable repetitions and reward beneficial crop sequences.

One of the most important aspects of AERIS is that it does not simply recommend a crop based on a single parameter. It considers the relationship between environmental conditions, seasonal requirements and the sequence in which crops are grown. It also tracks data availability and identifies areas where evidence is incomplete, instead of presenting every recommendation as equally reliable.

The project is developed primarily using Python. We use libraries such as NumPy and Pandas for numerical computation and data processing, Rasterio for handling geospatial raster datasets, Shapely and PyProj for spatial geometry and coordinate transformations, and Matplotlib and Tkinter for visualisation and the desktop interface. The system includes a Scientist Workbench for inspecting environmental evidence, crop suitability, rotation candidates and algorithm performance. A separate farmer-facing web interface is being developed to translate approved recommendations into simple, understandable explanations, making the results more accessible to non-technical users.

What makes AERIS distinctive is the integration of geospatial data processing, agricultural knowledge and evolutionary optimisation into one workflow. Instead of producing a generic crop recommendation, it attempts to explain why a particular crop rotation is preferred and how the available environmental evidence influenced that decision.

Our broader objective is to make agricultural planning more systematic, transparent and responsive to local environmental conditions. AERIS is currently a research prototype, and its recommendations are intended as preliminary decision support rather than a replacement for field soil testing or professional agricultural advice. With further validation and additional local data, the system could be extended to support more detailed, farm-level agricultural planning. The produced results can be fed again into AERIS to make a self feeding improving loop.
